It refers to the intrinsic nature of the faculty of joy, matter (*rūpa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) of mind-dissociated formations (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*).
What is being asked here?

It means that when one excludes phenomena associated with perception (*saṃjñā*) and those dissociated from the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), all phenomena— namely the eighteen elements (*dhātu*),
the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*)— are thereby excluded.
The eighteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*) associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) and dissociated from perception (*saṃjñā*).
What is included within that which is associated with the faculty of joy?
It refers to the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), namely the three elements, two bases, and three aggregates.
What constitutes the remainder?

It refers to the intrinsic nature of the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), form (*rūpa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*) that are dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*).
What is included in that which is dissociated from perception (*saṃjñā*)?

It refers to the intrinsic nature of perception, form (*rūpa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and the eleven factors of mental non-associated formations (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*); that is, eleven elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and three aggregates (*skandha*).
What is being asked here?

It means: excluding those factors associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) and those dissociated from perception (*saṃjñā*), one excludes all phenomena—that is, the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*).
Just as with the application of perception (*saṃjñā*) to the faculty of joy (*sukhendriya*), it is the same for its application to the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).

As for the application of volition (*cetanā*) to vitarka, vicāra, the factors associated with consciousness, the six groups of consciousness, the six groups of contact, and the six groups of volition—all are as explained in the section on feeling (*vedanā*); one should only state "perception" in place of "feeling."
The eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates that are associated with perception (*saṃjñā*) but dissociated from feeling (*vedanā*) born of eye-contact.
What do those associated with perception comprise?
This refers to the mind, the mental factors, the eight elements, the two bases, and the three aggregates.
What constitutes the remainder?
It refers to the intrinsic nature of perception, form, the unconditioned, and the eleven elements, eleven bases, and three aggregates that are dissociated from the mind.
What is included in that which is dissociated from feeling produced by eye-contact?
It refers to the intrinsic nature of feeling produced by eye-contact, form, the unconditioned, the seventeen elements of mental non-associated formations, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates.
What is being asked here?
It means that, excluding those phenomena associated with perception (*saṃjñā*) and those dissociated from feeling (*vedanā*) born of eye-contact, one excludes all phenomena:
namely, the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*).
The eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates associated with feeling born of eye-contact, but dissociated from perception.
By what are those associated with feeling born of eye-contact subsumed?
That is to say, mind and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma), the three realms (dhātu), the two bases (āyatana), and the three aggregates (skandha). What remains?

That is to say, the intrinsic nature of feeling produced by eye-contact, form (rūpa), the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), and seventeen elements (dhātu), twelve bases (āyatana), and five aggregates (skandha) consisting of formations dissociated from mind (citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra).
What is included in that which is dissociated from perception?
It refers to the intrinsic nature of perception, form, the unconditioned, the eleven elements of mental non-associated formations, the eleven bases, and the three aggregates.
What is being asked here?
It means that, excluding those phenomena associated with feeling produced by eye-contact and dissociated from perception, one excludes all phenomena:
the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates.

Just as with the application of perception (*saṃjñā*) to the feeling born of eye-contact, so it is for those born of contact through the ear, nose, tongue, body, and up to mind-contact; the detailed exposition should be understood accordingly.

In the sixth section of the second chapter, "Analysis of Categories," the sixth section concerns the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*) that are associated with volition (*cetanā*) but dissociated from contact (*sparśa*).
With what are those associated with volition (cetanā) comprised?
They are comprised of the eight elements (dhātu), two bases (āyatana), and four aggregates (skandha).
What remains [unincluded] therein?

That is to say: the intrinsic nature of volition (*cetanā*), form (*rūpa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and the eleven elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*) of formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*).
With what are those dissociated from contact (*sparśa*) subsumed?
It refers to the intrinsic nature of contact, form, the unconditioned, the eleven elements, the eleven bases, and the two aggregates of formations dissociated from mind.
What is being asked here?
That is to say, excluding those factors associated with volition (*cetanā*) and dissociated from contact (*sparśa*), one excludes all phenomena:
the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*).
[The remainder are] the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates that are associated with contact and dissociated from volition.
With what are those associated with contact included?
They are comprised of the eight elements, two bases, and four aggregates that are mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma).
What remains as the remainder?
That is to say: the intrinsic nature of contact, form, the unconditioned, and the eleven elements, eleven bases, and two aggregates of formations dissociated from mind.
With what are those dissociated from volition subsumed?

That is to say: the intrinsic nature of volition (*cetanā*), form (*rūpa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and the eleven elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*) that are dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*).
What is being asked here?
This means that, excluding those factors associated with contact (*sparśa*) and dissociated from volition (*cetanā*), one excludes all phenomena:
namely, the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*).
Just as volition is related to contact, so it is for each [mental factor] up to wisdom (*prajñā*).
Regarding the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*) that are associated with volition (*cetanā*) and dissociated from lack of faith (*āśraddhya*):
what is included within those associated with volition?
It refers to the eight elements, two bases, and four aggregates consisting of mind and mental factors.
What are the remaining [factors]?

They are the intrinsic nature of volition (*cetanā*), form (*rūpa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and the eleven elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*) of formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*).
What is comprised by that which is non-associated with lack of faith?
It refers to the intrinsic nature of lack of faith, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates of formations dissociated from mind.
What is being asked here?
It means that, excluding those phenomena associated with volition (*cetanā*) and dissociated from lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), one excludes all phenomena:
namely, the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*).
The eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates that are associated with lack of faith but dissociated from volition:
by what are those associated with lack of faith subsumed?
They are said to be comprised of the eight elements, two bases, and four aggregates consisting of the mind and mental factors.
What are the remaining factors?

They are the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates, excluding the intrinsic nature of non-faith, form, and unconditioned phenomena, as well as the formations dissociated from mind.
What is included in that which is dissociated from volition (*cetanā*)?

It refers to the intrinsic nature of volition, form (*rūpa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the eleven elements (*dhātu*) of mind-dissociated formations (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*), the eleven bases (*āyatana*), and the two aggregates (*skandha*).
What is being asked here?
It means that, excluding those phenomena associated with lack of faith and dissociated from volition, one excludes all phenomena:
namely, the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates.

As it is with volition (cetanā) in relation to lack of faith (āśraddhya), so it is in relation to the other universal defilements (mahākleśabhūmika-dharma), sensual desire (kāmarāga), hatred (dveṣa), the contact of ignorance (avidyā-sparśa), the contact that is neither knowledge nor ignorance (naivavidyā-nāvidyā-sparśa), and lack of shame (āhrīkya) and lack of dread (anapatrāpya).
Regarding those associated with volition (*cetanā*) and those dissociated from anger (*krodha*), there are eighteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*).
What is included within those associated with volition?
They are comprised of eight elements, two bases, and four aggregates, namely, the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).
What are the remaining factors?

They are the intrinsic nature of volition (*cetanā*), form (*rūpa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and the eleven elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*) that are dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*).
What is included [within the category] of that which is dissociated from anger?
It refers to the intrinsic nature of anger, form, the unconditioned, and the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates of formations dissociated from mind.
What is being asked here?
It means that, excluding those phenomena associated with volition (*cetanā*) and those dissociated from anger (*krodha*), one excludes all phenomena:
the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*).
The eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates that are associated with anger (*krodha*) but not associated with volition (*cetanā*).
What is included in those associated with anger?
They are comprised of the three elements, two bases, and four aggregates consisting of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
What are the remaining factors?
They are the intrinsic nature of anger, form, the unconditioned, the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates that are dissociated from mind.
What is included in that which is dissociated from volition?
It refers to the intrinsic nature of volition, form, the unconditioned, the eleven elements, the eleven bases, and the two aggregates of formations dissociated from mind.
What is being asked here?
It means that, excluding those phenomena associated with anger and dissociated from volition, all phenomena are excluded:
namely, the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates.

As it is with volition (cetanā) in relation to anger, so it is in relation to the other minor defilements (parīttakleśabhūmika), attachment to the formless (ārūpyarāga), doubt (vicikitsā), the five views (dṛṣṭi), contact of clear knowledge (vidyā-saṃsparśa), and the six groups of craving (ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇākāya).
The eighteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*) that are associated with volition (*cetanā*) but dissociated from attachment to form (*rūparāga*).
What is included within those associated with volition?
Namely, the eight elements, two bases, and four aggregates consisting of mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).
What are the remaining [factors]?

They are the intrinsic nature of volition (*cetanā*), form (*rūpa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and the eleven elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*) of formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*).
What is included in that which is dissociated from desire for form?
It refers to the intrinsic nature of desire for form, form, the unconditioned, and the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates of formations dissociated from mind.
What is being asked here?
It means that, excluding those phenomena associated with volition (*cetanā*) and those dissociated from attachment to form (*rūparāga*), one excludes all phenomena:
namely, the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*).
Regarding the eighteen elements (dhātus), twelve bases (āyatanas), and five aggregates (skandhas) that are associated with desire for form (rūparāga) but not associated with volition (cetanā):
what do those associated with desire for form include?
They are said to be the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma), comprising six elements, two bases, and four aggregates.
What are the remaining factors?
They are the intrinsic nature of desire for form, form, the unconditioned, the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates that are dissociated from mind.
What is the inclusion of that which is dissociated from volition?
It refers to the intrinsic nature of volition, form, the unconditioned, the eleven elements, the eleven bases, and the two aggregates of formations dissociated from mind.
What is being asked here?
It means that when one excludes those phenomena associated with desire for form (*rūparāga*) and dissociated from volition (*cetanā*), one excludes all phenomena:
namely, the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*).
The eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates associated with volition (*cetanā*) but dissociated from impingement-contact (*sapratigha-sparśa*).
What is included within those associated with volition?
They are the eight elements, two bases, and four aggregates consisting of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
What are the remaining [factors]?

They are the intrinsic nature of volition (*cetanā*), form (*rūpa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and the eleven elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*) that are dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*).
What is included in that which is dissociated from contact with resistance?
It refers to the intrinsic nature of contact with resistance, form, the unconditioned, and the thirteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates of formations dissociated from mind.
What is being asked here?
It means that, excluding those factors associated with volition (*cetanā*) and dissociated from impingement-contact (*pratigha-saṃsparśa*), one excludes all phenomena:
namely, the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*).
There are eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates that are associated with contact through resistance (*pratigha-saṃsparśa*) but dissociated from volition (*cetanā*).
What is included within those associated with contact through resistance?
This refers to the mind, the mental factors, seven elements, two bases, and four aggregates.
What remains?
It refers to the intrinsic nature of impingement-contact, form, the unconditioned, and the thirteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates that are dissociated from the mind.
What is included in that which is dissociated from volition (*cetanā*)?

It refers to the intrinsic nature of volition, form (*rūpa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the eleven elements (*dhātu*), the eleven bases (*āyatana*), and the two aggregates (*skandha*) of formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*).
What is being asked here?

It means that, excluding those phenomena associated with contact involving resistance (*sapratigha-sparśa-saṃprayukta*) and dissociated from volition (*cetanā-viprayukta*), one excludes all phenomena:
namely, the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*).
The eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates that are associated with volition (*cetanā*) but dissociated from the contact of designation (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*).
Those associated with volition are as previously described, up to two aggregates.
The dissociation from the designation-contact (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*) is as previously explained, up to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Just as with the association with volition (*cetanā*) and dissociation from the designation-contact, so too should the association with the designation-contact and dissociation from volition be explained in detail according to what is appropriate.

[The state] associated with volition (*cetanā*) but not associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), or associated with the faculty of pleasure but not associated with volition—these should be explained in detail according to the appropriate cases.
Just as volition is contrasted with the faculty of pleasure, it is likewise contrasted with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

[The state] associated with volition (*cetanā*) and dissociated from the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), and [the state] associated with the faculty of suffering and dissociated from volition—these should be explained in detail according to what is appropriate.

[The state] associated with volition and dissociated from the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), and [the state] associated with the faculty of joy and dissociated from volition—these should be explained in detail according to what is appropriate.
As with volition (*cetanā*) in relation to the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), so it is in relation to the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).

Volition should be explained in detail as it applies to applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), the factors of consciousness (*vijñāna-dharma*), the six groups of consciousness (*ṣaḍ-vijñānakāya*), the six groups of contact (*ṣaṭ-sparśakāya*), the six groups of feeling (*ṣaṭ-vedanākāya*), and the six groups of perception (*ṣaṭ-saṃjñākāya*), according to what is appropriate.
*Abhidharmadhātupāda-śāstra*, Middle Fascicle;
*Abhidharmadhātupāda-śāstra*, Lower Fascicle.
Composed by the Venerable Vasumitra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under Imperial Decree. Section Seven:

The Analysis of the Correspondence of the Eighteen Dhātus, Twelve Āyatanas, and Five Skandhas with Contact (sparśa) and the Non-correspondence with Attention (manasikāra). Part Two, Section Seven. Contact (sparśa) Correspondence and Attention (manasikāra) Non-correspondence. The eighteen dhātus, twelve āyatanas, and five skandhas.
Contact-associated factors are as previously described, up to the two aggregates (*skandha*).
What is included in those that are non-associated with attention (*manasikāra*)?

They consist of the intrinsic nature of attention, form (*rūpa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and the eleven elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and two aggregates of the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*).
What is being asked here?
It means that if one excludes those phenomena associated with contact (*sparśa*) and dissociated from attention (*manasikāra*), one excludes all phenomena:
namely, the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*).
The eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates that are associated with attention (*manasikāra*) but dissociated from contact (*sparśa*).
What is included in those associated with attention?
They are the eight elements, two bases, and four aggregates consisting of mind and mental factors.
What are the remaining [factors]?

They are the intrinsic nature of attention (*manasikāra*), form (*rūpa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and the eleven elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*) of formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*).
The dissociation from contact and so forth are as previously explained.
Just as contact is treated in relation to attention (*manasikāra*), the same applies up to its treatment in relation to wisdom (*prajñā*).

One should explain in detail, as appropriate, the association of contact with non-faith (*āśraddhya*) and the dissociation of non-faith from contact, as well as the association of non-faith and the dissociation from contact.

Just as with contact (*sparśa*) in relation to lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), so it is in relation to the other universal defilements (*mahākleśabhūmika*), sensual desire (*kāmarāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*).
One should explain in detail, as appropriate, how contact is associated (*saṃprayukta*) while anger (*krodha*) is dissociated (*viprayukta*), and how anger is associated while contact is dissociated.

As it is with contact (*sparśa*) in relation to anger (*krodha*), so it is in relation to the other minor defilement-ground factors (*parīttakleśabhūmika-dharma*), attachment to the formless (*ārūpyarāga*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), the five views (*pañcadṛṣṭi*), and the six groups of craving (*ṣaṭtṛṣṇākāya*).

One should explain in detail, as appropriate, that which is associated with contact but not associated with attachment to form (*rūparāga*), and that which is associated with attachment to form but not associated with contact.

Contact is associated with [the mind] but not associated with the faculty of pleasure; the faculty of pleasure is associated with [the mind] but not associated with contact. This should be explained in detail according to what is appropriate.
Just as contact is treated in relation to the faculty of pleasure, it is the same when treated in relation to the faculty of equanimity.

Contact is associated with [the aggregate of feeling], but not with the faculty of pain; the faculty of pain is associated with it, but not with contact. This should be explained in detail as appropriate.

Contact is associated with [the aggregate of feeling], but not with the faculty of joy; the faculty of joy is associated with it, but not with contact. This should be explained in detail as appropriate.
Just as contact is related to the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*), so too is it related to the faculty of grief (*domanassindriya*).

Contact should be explained in detail in relation to applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), the factors of consciousness (*viññāṇadhamma*), the six groups of consciousness (*cha viññāṇakāyā*), the six groups of feeling (*cha vedanākāyā*), the six groups of perception (*cha saññākāyā*), and the six groups of volition (*cha cetanākāyā*), according to what is appropriate in each case.

The Eighth Section of the Second Chapter on Analysis: The Eighteenth Section on the Correspondence with Mental Attention (*manasikāra*) and Non-correspondence with Desire (*chanda*) regarding the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*).
The association with attention (*manasikāra*) and so forth is as previously explained.
With what are those dissociated from desire (*kāma-viprayukta*) subsumed?

They are: the intrinsic nature of desire, form (*rūpa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and the eleven elements (*dhātu*), eleven bases (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*) of the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
What is being asked here?
As previously stated:
the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates associated with desire, but not associated with attention.
With what are those associated with desire comprised?
They are comprised of the eight elements, two bases, and four aggregates that are mind and mental factors.
What remains besides these?
This refers to the intrinsic nature of desire, form, the unconditioned, the eleven elements, the eleven bases, and the two aggregates of formations dissociated from mind.
The dissociation from attention and so forth is as previously explained.
Just as with attention (*manasikāra*) in relation to desire, so it is up to its relation to wisdom (*prajñā*).

One should explain in detail, as appropriate, [the cases of] that which is associated with attention but not associated with lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), and that which is associated with lack of faith but not associated with attention.

Just as with attention (*manasikāra*) in relation to lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), so it is in relation to the other universal afflictive mental factors (*mahākleśabhūmika-dharma*), sensual desire (*kāmarāga*), hatred (*pratigha*), the contact of ignorance (*avidyā-sparśa*), the contact of neither-ignorance-nor-non-ignorance (*naivavidyānāvidyā-sparśa*), and lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*).

Mental attention (*manasikāra*) is associated with anger (*krodha*), but not vice versa; anger is associated with mental attention, but not vice versa. This should be explained in detail according to the appropriate cases.

Just as mental attention is treated in relation to anger, the same applies when it is related to the other minor defilements (*upakleśa-bhūmika-dharma*), attachment to the formless (*ārūpya-rāga*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), the five views (*dṛṣṭi*), contact through clear knowledge (*vidyā-saṃsparśa*), and the six groups of craving (*ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇā-kāya*).

That which is associated with attention (*manasikāra*) but not associated with desire for form (*rūparāga*), and that which is associated with desire for form but not associated with attention—these should be explained in detail as appropriate.

That which is associated with attention but not associated with impingement-contact (*pratigha-sparśa*), and that which is associated with impingement-contact but not associated with attention—these should be explained in detail as appropriate.

It should be explained in detail as appropriate: [there are cases where] there is association with attention (manasikāra) but non-association with designation-contact (adhivacana-saṃsparśa), and [cases where] there is association with designation-contact but non-association with attention.

That which is associated with attention (*manasikāra*) but not associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), and that which is associated with the faculty of pleasure but not associated with attention—these should be explained in detail according to the appropriate cases.
Just as [this analysis] was applied to the faculty of pleasure in relation to attention, it is likewise applied to the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

That which is associated with attention (*manasikāra*) but not associated with the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), and that which is associated with the faculty of suffering but not associated with attention—these should be explained in detail according to their respective applications.

That which is associated with attention but not associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), and that which is associated with the faculty of joy but not associated with attention—these should also be explained in detail according to their respective applications.
Just as mental attention is applied to the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), so it is with the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).

Mental attention is likewise applied to vitarka, vicāra, consciousness-phenomena, the six groups of consciousness, the six groups of contact, the six groups of feeling, the six groups of perception, and the six groups of volition; these should be explained in detail according to their respective applications.

The Ninth Gate: Within the second chapter on "Discrimination," the ninth gate concerns the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates that are associated with desire but dissociated from resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).
The association with desire and so forth are as previously explained.
What is included within that which is dissociated from resolve (*adhimokṣa*)?
It refers to the intrinsic nature of resolve, form, the unconditioned, the eleven elements, the eleven bases, and the two aggregates of formations dissociated from mind.
What is being asked here?
It means that, excluding those phenomena associated with desire and dissociated from resolve, one excludes all phenomena:
the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates.
The eighteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*) that are associated with resolve (*adhimokṣa*) but dissociated from desire (*chanda*).
What is included within those associated with resolve?
They are the eight elements, two bases, and four aggregates consisting of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
What are the remaining [factors]?

They are the nature of resolve (*adhimukti-svabhāva*), form (*rūpa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the eleven elements (*dhātu*) that are formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*), the eleven bases (*āyatana*), and the two aggregates (*skandha*).
The dissociation from desire and so forth are as previously explained.
Just as with the opposition of desire to resolve (adhimokṣa), the same applies to its opposition to mindfulness (smṛti), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (prajñā).

One should explain in detail, as appropriate, the cases of association with desire and dissociation from lack of faith (āśraddhya), and the cases of association with lack of faith and dissociation from desire.

Just as desire is related to lack of faith, so it is with the other universal afflictive mental factors (*mahākleśabhūmika-dharma*), sensual desire, hatred, the contact of ignorance, the contact of neither-ignorance-nor-non-ignorance, and lack of shame and lack of dread.
Desire is associated with it, while anger is not; anger is associated with it, while desire is not. This should be explained in detail according to what is appropriate.

Just as desire is contrasted with anger, the same applies when contrasting it with the other minor defilement-ground factors (*parīttakleśabhūmika*), attachment to the formless (*ārūpyarāga*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), the five views (*dṛṣṭi*), contact through knowledge (*vidyā-saṃsparśa*), and the six groups of craving (*ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇākāya*).

That which is associated with desire but not associated with attachment to form, and that which is associated with attachment to form but not associated with desire—these should be explained in detail as appropriate.

That which is associated with desire but not associated with impingement-contact (*pratigha-sparśa*), and that which is associated with impingement-contact but not associated with desire—these should be explained in detail as appropriate.

Those associated with desire but dissociated from the contact of designation (*adhivacanasaṃsparśa*), and those associated with the contact of designation but dissociated from desire, should be explained in detail according to their respective applications.

Those associated with desire but dissociated from the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), and those associated with the faculty of pleasure but dissociated from desire, should be explained in detail according to their respective applications.
Just as desire is related to the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), so too is it related to the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

Desire is associated with [the faculty] but not associated with the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*); the faculty of suffering is associated with [the faculty] but not associated with desire. This should be explained in detail according to what is appropriate for each case.

That which is associated with desire but not associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), and that which is associated with the faculty of joy but not associated with desire—these should be explained in detail as appropriate.
Just as desire is contrasted with the faculty of joy, it is likewise contrasted with the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).

One should explain in detail, as appropriate, how desire relates to vitarka, vicāra, the factors of consciousness, the six groups of consciousness, the six groups of contact, the six groups of feeling, the six groups of perception, and the six groups of volition.
The Tenth Gate within the Second Chapter, "Analysis," concerning the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates that correspond with resolve but do not correspond with mindfulness.
The association with resolve (*adhimokṣa*) and so forth are as previously explained.
With what are those dissociated from mindfulness (*smṛti*) subsumed?

They are the intrinsic nature of mindfulness, form (*rūpa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and the eleven factors of the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*); that is, the eleven elements (*dhātu*), the eleven bases (*āyatana*), and two aggregates (*skandha*).
What is being asked here?
As previously stated:
the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates that are associated with mindfulness but dissociated from resolve.
With what are those associated with mindfulness comprised?
They are comprised of the mind, the mental factors, eight elements, two bases, and four aggregates.
What remains besides these?
That is to say: the nature of mindfulness, form, the unconditioned, the eleven elements, the eleven bases, and two aggregates among the formations dissociated from mind.
Its non-association with resolve and so forth is as previously explained.
As with resolve (*adhimokṣa*) in relation to mindfulness (*smṛti*), so it is in relation to concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
One should explain in detail, as appropriate, how resolve is associated and lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) is dissociated, and how lack of faith is associated and resolve is dissociated.

Just as with resolve (*adhimokṣa*) in relation to lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), so it is in relation to the other universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*), sensual desire (*kāmarāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), the contact of ignorance (*avidyā-sparśa*), the contact of neither-ignorance-nor-non-ignorance (*naivavidyā-nāvidyā-sparśa*), lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*).
Adhimokṣa (resolute confidence) is associated with it, while krodha (anger) is not; krodha is associated with it, while adhimokṣa is not. This should be explained in detail as appropriate.

Just as [the relationship] is established between adhimokṣa and krodha, so it is for the other *parītta-kleśa-bhūmika* dharmas (minor defilement-ground factors), rāga-rūpya (desire for the formless), vicikitsā (doubt), the five *dṛṣṭi*s (views), vidyā-saṃsparśa (contact with knowledge), and the six *tṛṣṇā-kāya*s (bodies of craving).

That which is associated with resolve (*adhimokṣa*) but not associated with greed for form (*rūparāga*), and that which is associated with greed for form but not associated with resolve, should be explained in detail as appropriate.

That which is associated with resolve but not associated with impingement-contact (*pratighasparśa*), and that which is associated with impingement-contact but not associated with resolve, should be explained in detail as appropriate.

That which is associated with resolve but not associated with designation-contact, and that which is associated with designation-contact but not associated with resolve—these should be explained in detail as appropriate.

Those associated with resolve (*adhimokṣa*) but not associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), and those associated with the faculty of pleasure but not associated with resolve, should be explained in detail as appropriate.
Just as resolve is treated in relation to the faculty of pleasure, the same applies to its treatment in relation to the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

Those associated with resolve (adhimokṣa) but not associated with the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya), and those associated with the faculty of suffering but not associated with resolve, should be explained in detail as appropriate.

Those associated with resolve but not associated with the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya), and those associated with the faculty of joy but not associated with resolve, should be explained in detail as appropriate.
Just as with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), so it is with the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).

As with the faculty of resolve (*adhimokṣa*), so it should be explained in detail as appropriate for its correspondence with applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), the factors of consciousness, the six groups of consciousness, the six groups of contact, the six groups of feeling, the six groups of perception, and the six groups of volition (*cetanā*).
The Eleventh Section of the Second Chapter on Classification: The Eighteen Elements, Twelve Bases, and Five Aggregates Associated with Mindfulness but Not Associated with Samādhi.
The association with mindfulness and so forth is as previously explained.
What is included in that which is dissociated from samādhi?

It consists of the intrinsic nature of samādhi, form, the unconditioned, and the eleven factors of the formations dissociated from mind; that is, the eleven elements (dhātus), the eleven bases (āyatanas), and two aggregates (skandhas).
What is being asked here?
It is as previously stated:
the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates that are associated with samādhi but dissociated from mindfulness.
With what are those associated with samādhi comprised?
They are the eight elements, two bases, and four aggregates consisting of mind and mental factors.
What remains besides these?
That is to say: the intrinsic nature of samādhi, form, the unconditioned, the eleven elements (dhātus), the eleven bases (āyatanas), and two aggregates (skandhas).
The dissociation from mindfulness and so forth are as previously explained.
Just as mindfulness is contrasted with samādhi, so it is with wisdom.

One should explain in detail, as appropriate, how mindfulness is associated [with certain factors] and dissociated from lack of faith, and how lack of faith is associated [with certain factors] and dissociated from mindfulness.

Just as mindfulness is opposed to lack of faith, so too is it opposed to the other universal afflictive mental factors (*mahākleśabhūmika-dharma*), sensual desire, hatred, the contact of ignorance, the contact of neither-ignorance-nor-non-ignorance, lack of shame, and lack of dread.

Mindfulness is associated [with certain factors] and dissociated from anger; anger is associated [with certain factors] and dissociated from mindfulness. This should be explained in detail as appropriate.

Just as mindfulness is treated in relation to anger, the same applies when it is treated in relation to the other minor defilement-ground factors (*parītta-kleśa-bhūmika*), attachment to the formless (*ārūpya-rāga*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), the five views (*dṛṣṭi*), contact with knowledge (*vidyā-saṃsparśa*), and the six groups of craving (*ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇā-kāya*).

Mindfulness is associated [with certain factors] but not associated with greed for form; greed for form is associated [with certain factors] but not associated with mindfulness. This should be explained in detail according to what is appropriate.

Mindfulness is associated [with certain factors] but not associated with impingement-contact; impingement-contact is associated [with certain factors] but not associated with mindfulness. This should be explained in detail according to what is appropriate.

[The factors] associated with mindfulness but not associated with the contact of designation (adhivacana-saṃsparśa), and those associated with the contact of designation but not associated with mindfulness, should be explained in detail according to what is appropriate.

[The factors] associated with mindfulness but not associated with the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya), and those associated with the faculty of pleasure but not associated with mindfulness, should be explained in detail according to what is appropriate.
Just as mindfulness is related to the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), so it is with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

Mindfulness is associated [with the faculty of pleasure] but not associated with the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*); the faculty of pain is associated [with the faculty of pleasure] but not associated with mindfulness. This should be explained in detail according to what is appropriate.

Mental application (*smṛti*) may be associated with it, while the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) may not; the faculty of joy may be associated with it, while mental application may not. This should be explained in detail according to what is appropriate.
Just as mental application is treated in relation to the faculty of joy, so it is also in relation to the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).

One should explain in detail, as appropriate, how mindfulness relates to vitarka, vicāra, the factors of consciousness, the six groups of consciousness, the six groups of contact, the six groups of feeling, the six groups of perception, and the six groups of volition.

The Twelfth Gate: Within the Second Chapter on Analysis, the Twelfth Gate concerning the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), twelve bases (*āyatanas*), and five aggregates (*skandhas*) associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and dissociated from wisdom (*prajñā*).
The association with samādhi and so forth are as previously explained.
What is included in that which is dissociated from wisdom (*prajñā*)?

It refers to the intrinsic nature of wisdom, form, the unconditioned, the eleven elements (*dhātu*), the eleven bases (*āyatana*), and the two aggregates (*skandha*) of formations dissociated from mind.
What is being asked here?
It is as previously stated:
the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates that are associated with wisdom but not associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
With what are those associated with wisdom (prajñā-saṃprayukta) subsumed?
They are the eight elements (dhātu), two bases (āyatana), and four aggregates (skandha) consisting of mind and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma).
What remains [unsubsumed] by these?

That is to say: the intrinsic nature of wisdom (*prajñā-svabhāva*), form (*rūpa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), the eleven elements (*dhātu*) and eleven bases (*āyatana*) that are dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), and two aggregates (*skandha*).
The details regarding those dissociated from meditative concentration (*samādhi-viprayukta*) are as previously explained.
One associated with samādhi is not associated with lack of faith; one associated with lack of faith is not associated with samādhi. This should be explained in detail as appropriate for each case.

As it is with samādhi in relation to lack of faith, so it is in relation to the other universal defilements (mahākleśabhūmika), sensual desire, hatred, the contact of ignorance, the contact of neither-knowledge-nor-ignorance, and lack of shame and lack of dread.
Concentration (*samādhi*) is associated with and dissociated from anger (*krodha*); anger is associated with and dissociated from concentration. This should be explained in detail as appropriate.

Just as it is with concentration in relation to anger, so it is for the other minor defilements (*upakleśa*), attachment to the formless (*ārūpyarāga*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), the five views (*dṛṣṭi*), contact of clarity (*vidyā-saṃsparśa*), and the six groups of craving (*ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇākāya*).

That which is associated with samādhi but not associated with desire for form, and that which is associated with desire for form but not associated with samādhi; these should be explained in detail as appropriate.

It should be explained in detail as appropriate: that which is associated with samādhi but dissociated from impingement-contact (pratigha-sparśa), and that which is associated with impingement-contact but dissociated from samādhi.

It should be explained in detail as appropriate: that which is associated with samādhi but not associated with adhivacana-saṃsparśa, and that which is associated with adhivacana-saṃsparśa but not associated with samādhi.

It should be explained in detail as appropriate: that which is associated with samādhi but not associated with the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya), and that which is associated with the faculty of pleasure but not associated with samādhi.
Just as it is with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) in relation to concentration (*samādhi*), so it is with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

One should explain in detail, as appropriate, that which is associated with concentration but not associated with the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), and that which is associated with the faculty of suffering but not associated with concentration.

That which is associated with samādhi but not associated with the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya), and that which is associated with the faculty of joy but not associated with samādhi—these should be explained in detail as appropriate.
Just as with *samādhi* in relation to the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*), so it is in relation to the faculty of grief (*domanassindriya*).

One should explain in detail, as appropriate, how *samādhi* relates to applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), the factors of consciousness, the six groups of consciousness, the six groups of contact, the six groups of feeling, the six groups of perception, and the six groups of volition.

The Thirteenth Gate: Within the second chapter, "Analysis," this is the thirteenth gate concerning the association with wisdom and non-association with lack of faith, and the association with lack of faith and non-association with wisdom; these should be explained in detail as appropriate.

Just as wisdom relates to lack of faith, so it is with respect to the other universal afflictive mental factors (*mahākleśabhūmika*), sensual desire, hatred, the contact of ignorance, the contact of neither-ignorance-nor-non-ignorance, lack of shame, and lack of dread.
Wisdom is associated with [the other factors] but not with anger; anger is associated with them but not with wisdom. This should be explained in detail as appropriate.

Just as wisdom is treated in relation to anger, so it is for the remaining minor defilements (*upakleśa*), attachment to the formless (*ārūpyarāga*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), the five views (*dṛṣṭi*), contact through clear knowledge (*vidyā-saṃsparśa*), and the six groups of craving (*ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇākāya*).

[The case where] there is association with wisdom but no association with desire for form, and [the case where] there is association with desire for form but no association with wisdom, should be explained in detail as appropriate.

[The case where] there is association with wisdom but no association with tangible contact, and [the case where] there is association with tangible contact but no association with wisdom, should be explained in detail as appropriate.

[The case of] association with wisdom (prajñā) and non-association with the contact of designation (adhivacanasaṃsparśa), and [the case of] association with the contact of designation and non-association with wisdom, should be explained in detail according to what is appropriate.

[The case of] association with wisdom and non-association with the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya), and [the case of] association with the faculty of pleasure and non-association with wisdom, should be explained in detail according to what is appropriate.
Just as with wisdom in relation to the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), so it is in relation to the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
One should explain in detail, as appropriate, how wisdom is associated and the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*) is dissociated, and how the faculty of pain is associated and wisdom is dissociated.

Wisdom may be associated with [the faculty of] joy but not associated with the faculty of joy; the faculty of joy may be associated with wisdom but not associated with wisdom. This should be explained in detail according to what is appropriate.
As it is when wisdom is contrasted with the faculty of joy, so it is when it is contrasted with the faculty of grief.

One should explain in detail, as appropriate, how wisdom relates to vitarka, vicāra, the factors of consciousness, the six groups of consciousness, the six groups of contact, the six groups of feeling, the six groups of perception, and the six groups of volition.
The Fourteenth Gate: The Second Chapter on Analysis, Gate Fourteen—The Eighteen Elements, Twelve Bases, and Five Aggregates Associated with Lack of Faith and Dissociated from Laziness.
The association with lack of faith (*aśraddhyā*) and so forth are as previously explained.
What is included in that which is dissociated from laziness (*kausīdya*)?

It refers to the intrinsic nature of laziness, form (*rūpa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and five aggregates (*skandha*) of the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*).
What is being asked here?
It is as previously stated:
the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates associated with indolence and dissociated from lack of faith.
With what are those associated with laziness subsumed?
They are the mind, the mental factors, eight elements, two bases, and four aggregates.
What remains besides these?
That is to say: the intrinsic nature of indolence, form, the unconditioned, the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates that are dissociated from mind.
Non-faith and its associated dissociations are as previously explained.

Just as lack of faith is paired with laziness, so it is with the other universal mental factors of great affliction (*mahākleśabhūmika*), sensual desire, hatred, contact associated with ignorance, contact associated with neither-knowledge-nor-ignorance, lack of shame, and lack of dread.

Lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) is associated with anger (*krodha*) and dissociated from it; anger is associated with lack of faith and dissociated from it. This should be explained in detail as appropriate.

Just as lack of faith is treated in relation to anger, the same applies when it is related to the other minor defilements (*upakleśa-bhūmika-dharma*), attachment to the formless (*ārūpyarāga*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), the five views (*dṛṣṭi*), contact through clear knowledge (*vidyā-saṃsparśa*), and the six groups of craving (*ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇākāya*).

That which is associated with lack of faith (āśraddhya) but not associated with desire for form (rūparāga), and that which is associated with desire for form but not associated with lack of faith—these should be explained in detail as appropriate.

That which is associated with lack of faith but not associated with impingement-contact (pratigha-sparśa), and that which is associated with impingement-contact but not associated with lack of faith—these should also be explained in detail as appropriate.

That which is associated with lack of faith (āśraddhya) is not associated with the contact of designation (adhivacanasaṃsparśa); that which is associated with the contact of designation is not associated with lack of faith. This should be explained in detail as appropriate for each case.

Lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) is associated with [the faculty of] pleasure (*sukhendriya*) but not associated with the faculty of pleasure; the faculty of pleasure is associated with it but not associated with lack of faith. This should be explained in detail as appropriate.
Just as lack of faith is treated in relation to the faculty of pleasure, so it is also in relation to the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

That which is associated with lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) but not associated with the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*), and that which is associated with the faculty of suffering but not associated with lack of faith—these should be explained in detail as appropriate.

That which is associated with lack of faith but not associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), and that which is associated with the faculty of joy but not associated with lack of faith—these should be explained in detail as appropriate.
Just as with regard to the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), so it is with regard to the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).

As with regard to the faculty of lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), so it should be explained in detail as appropriate for its application to vitarka, vicāra, the factors of consciousness, the six groups of consciousness, the six groups of contact, the six groups of feeling, the six groups of perception, and the six groups of volition.

In this fifteenth section of the second chapter on "Discrimination," regarding these principles, one should appropriately contemplate the various distinctions such as indolence and so forth, based on the previously explained method of single-practice application (*ekāyana-upāya*).
Regarding the distinctions among these various categories, one should not speak of similar states that occupy different positions.
This applies even to the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates, such as those associated with visual consciousness and those dissociated from visual contact.
With what are the factors associated with visual consciousness subsumed?
They are comprised of one element, one base, and three aggregates.
What constitutes the remainder?

That is to say: the intrinsic nature of visual consciousness, visible forms, the unconditioned, and the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates that are dissociated from mental formations.
To which [categories] is that which is dissociated from eye-contact subsumed?
That is to say: the intrinsic nature of eye-contact, visible forms, the unconditioned, the seventeen elements that are formations dissociated from mind, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates.
What is being asked here?
That is to say, excluding those phenomena associated with visual consciousness and those not associated with visual contact, one excludes all phenomena:
the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates.
The eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates that are associated with eye-contact but dissociated from eye-consciousness:
by what are those factors associated with eye-contact subsumed?
This refers to the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma), which comprise three elements (dhātu), two bases (āyatana), and four aggregates (skandha). What remains?

It refers to the intrinsic nature of eye-contact, form (rūpa), unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta), and seventeen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates belonging to the formations dissociated from mind (cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra).
What is included that is not associated with visual consciousness?
It refers to the intrinsic nature of visual consciousness, form, the unconditioned, and the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates of formations dissociated from mind.
What is being asked here?
It means that if one excludes those phenomena associated with eye-contact and dissociated from eye-consciousness, one excludes all phenomena:
namely, the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates.
As with visual consciousness in relation to eye-contact, so it should be explained in detail as appropriate for everything up to mind-contact and the six groups of volition (*ṣaṭ-saṃskāra-kāya*).
[The eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates] that are associated with visual consciousness but dissociated from the feeling produced by eye-contact.
With what are eye-consciousness and its associated factors subsumed?
They are comprised of one element, one base, and three aggregates.
What remains besides these?

That is to say: the intrinsic nature of visual consciousness, visible forms, the unconditioned, the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates that are dissociated from feeling produced by eye-contact—by what are these included?
That is to say: the nature of feeling produced by eye-contact; form; the unconditioned; and seventeen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates belonging to the formations dissociated from mind.
What is being asked here?
It means that, excluding those factors associated with eye-consciousness and dissociated from feeling produced by eye-contact, one excludes all phenomena:
the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates.
The eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates that are associated with feeling born of eye-contact, but not associated with eye-consciousness.
What do those factors associated with feeling born of eye-contact comprise?
This refers to the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), which comprise three elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and three aggregates (*skandha*). What remains?

It refers to the nature of feeling (*vedanā*) produced by eye-contact, form (*rūpa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and seventeen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates belonging to the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*).
What is included in that which is dissociated from visual consciousness?
It refers to the intrinsic nature of visual consciousness, form, the unconditioned, and the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates of formations dissociated from mind.
What is being asked here?
It means that, excluding those phenomena associated with feeling produced by eye-contact and dissociated from eye-consciousness, one excludes all phenomena:
the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates.

Just as with visual consciousness in relation to the feeling produced by eye-contact, so it should be explained in detail, as appropriate, up to the feelings produced by mind-contact and the six groups of perception.
The eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates that are associated with eye-consciousness but dissociated from craving born of eye-contact.
What is included within those associated with eye-consciousness?
This refers to one element, one base, and three aggregates among the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*).
What constitutes the remainder?

It refers to the nature of visual consciousness, form, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates of formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*).
What is included in that which is dissociated from craving born of eye-contact?
It refers to the intrinsic nature of craving born of eye-contact, form, the unconditioned, the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates of formations dissociated from mind.
What is being asked here?
It means that, excluding those phenomena associated with eye-consciousness and those not associated with craving born of eye-contact, one excludes all phenomena:
the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates.
The eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates associated with craving born of eye-contact, but dissociated from eye-consciousness.
By what are those factors associated with craving born of eye-contact subsumed?
This refers to the mind and mental factors, the three realms, the two bases, and the four aggregates. What remains?
It refers to the nature of craving born of eye-contact, form, the unconditioned, and the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates of formations dissociated from mind.
What is included that is not associated with visual consciousness?
It refers to the intrinsic nature of visual consciousness, form, the unconditioned, the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates that are dissociated from mind.
What is being asked here?
It means that, excluding those phenomena associated with craving born of eye-contact and dissociated from visual consciousness, one excludes all phenomena:
the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates.
Just as it is with craving born of eye-contact in relation to visual consciousness, so it is for craving born of contact through the [other] sense bases up to the mind.

In the sixteenth section of the second chapter, "The Analysis of Categories," just as it was explained for the door of visual consciousness, so it should be explained in detail for the five doors up to mental consciousness, as appropriate.
As with the six groups of consciousness and the six gateways, so too should the six groups of contact and their six gateways be explained in detail as appropriate.
[This concerns] the eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates that are associated with feeling produced by eye-contact but dissociated from perception produced by eye-consciousness.
With what are the feelings produced by eye-contact associated?
They are comprised within the three realms, two bases, and three aggregates.
What remains besides these?
That is to say: the nature of feeling produced by eye-contact, form, the unconditioned, the seventeen elements that are formations dissociated from mind, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates.
What is included in that which is dissociated from the perception produced by eye-contact?

It refers to the intrinsic nature of the perception produced by eye-contact, form, the unconditioned, the seventeen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates that are formations dissociated from mind.
What is being asked here?
It means: excluding those phenomena associated with feeling born of eye-contact and dissociated from perception born of eye-contact, one excludes all phenomena:
namely, the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates.
The eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates that are associated with perception born of eye-contact and dissociated from feeling born of eye-contact:
by what are those factors associated with perception born of eye-contact subsumed?
This refers to the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), which comprise three elements (*dhātu*), two bases (*āyatana*), and three aggregates (*skandha*).
What constitutes the remainder?

It refers to the intrinsic nature of perception (*saṃjñā*) produced by eye-contact, as well as form (*rūpa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and seventeen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates belonging to the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*).
What is included in that which is dissociated from feeling born of eye-contact?
It refers to the intrinsic nature of feeling born of eye-contact, as well as form, the unconditioned, the seventeen elements of non-associated formations, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates.
What is being asked here?

It means: excluding those phenomena associated with the perception produced by eye-contact and dissociated from the feeling produced by eye-contact, one excludes all phenomena—the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas).
